hook: A teacher asks 25 students how many books they read over the summer. A list of 25 numbers says little. A row of dots over a number line says a lot at once: most students read 2 to 4 books, a few read many more, and one read none. Graphs for quantitative data put the values on a number line so you can see where they fall.

prereq.why: Books read is a count, so arithmetic with it makes sense.

prereq.q: Of 25 students, 12 read four books or more. What proportion is that?

figure.caption: The same 30 homework times as a dotplot and as histograms with bins 5 and 10 minutes wide. Narrow bins show detail; wide bins give a smoother picture.

chain.cause: Quantitative values have positions on a number line
chain.effect: a dotplot puts one dot per value above its place on the line

chain.cause: With many values, dots pile up
chain.effect: a histogram groups values into equal bins and draws a bar for each bin’s count

chain.cause: The bins are chosen by whoever draws the graph
chain.effect: the same data can look bumpy with narrow bins or smooth with wide ones

chain.cause: Adding up the relative frequencies from the left
chain.effect: a cumulative relative frequency graph shows the proportion of values at or below each point

ideas: A dotplot shows each value as a dot above a number line; repeated values stack. Best for small data sets.
A stemplot splits each value into a stem (leading digits) and a leaf (last digit). It keeps every value; always give a key.
A histogram groups values into equal bins; each bar’s height is the bin’s count or relative frequency, and the bars touch. Its look depends on the bin width.
A cumulative relative frequency graph gives, at each value, the proportion of the data at or below that value. The proportion between two values is the difference of the heights.

misconception.wrong: A value that lands on a bin edge, like 4 books in bins 2 to 4 and 4 to 6, is counted in both bins.
misconception.right: Each value goes in exactly one bin. With bins that hold their left end, 4 goes in the 4 to 6 bin.

summary: Dotplots and stemplots show every value of a small quantitative data set; histograms group values into equal bins and show the count in each, and their look depends on the bin width. A cumulative relative frequency graph shows the proportion of values at or below each point, so a proportion between two values is a difference of heights.
